\title{Bounding the Worst-Case Execution Time of an Industrial \ndt{} Scan Matcher:\\
a Counter-Guided, Cross-Language Approach}

\author{%
  \IEEEauthorblockN{Yuuki Takano}
  \IEEEauthorblockA{TIER IV, Inc.\\
  \todo{email / co-authors / affiliations}}
}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Iterative scan-matching kernels such as the Normal Distributions Transform (\ndt{}) sit on the
critical path of autonomous-vehicle localization, yet their execution time is strongly
data-dependent, which makes worst-case execution time (WCET) analysis with classical static
methods impractical. We present a hybrid WCET analysis of the Autoware \ndt{} scan matcher,
built around a bit-exact Rust port of the production C++ engine. Deterministic algorithmic cost
counters --- compiled to zero overhead when disabled --- serve both as machine-checked evidence
for a structural work bound and as a platform-independent fitness function for a worst-input
search; because the two implementations are bit-exact, a worst input found on the instrumented
Rust engine transfers verbatim to the uninstrumented C++ engine, with equal work certified by an
iteration-count assertion. On the frozen adversarial input set, the search provably saturates the
analytic kernel-evaluation bound ($P \cdot \maxnn \cdot (N_{\mathrm{iter}}{+}1)$). Measurements
show the Rust port meets or beats the C++ engine's observed maximum on every fixture
(max-latency ratios 0.14--0.86), while the C++ engine performs $\approx$11 heap allocations per
point per derivative pass ($\num{682248}$ per align on the worst fixture) against a proven zero
for Rust. A unit-cost regression ties median latency to the counters with $R^2 \ge 0.99$ on
both engines, a controlled sweep shows the bound is affine in the scan size, and a two-tier
formulation separates the untrusted-input worst case from the
preprocessing-reachable one ($5\times$ apart), quantifying the value of validating input
contracts at the component boundary. A Gumbel tail fit provides comparative \pwcet{} estimates.
\todo{AArch64 bare-metal target numbers (M5).}
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
WCET, measurement-based timing analysis, extreme value theory, Rust, scan matching, NDT,
autonomous driving, localization
\end{IEEEkeywords}
